title: Foraging crab apples for jelly and juice
subtitle: ID, harvest window, and native vs ornamental
excerpt: Crab apple fruits on hedgerow trees and in scrubland across the UK from August through October. The small, tart fruits are too acid to eat raw in quantity but cook into a firm, jewel-pink jelly or tart juice. Distinguish native crab apple from the ornamental crabs planted in parks.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); BSBI species accounts for Malus sylvestris; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Crab apple (Malus sylvestris) grows in hedgerows, scrubland, and the edges of ancient woodland across the UK, fruiting from August through October. The fruit is small, 2 to 4 cm across, and very acid and astringent to eat raw, but it cooks into a firm, clear jelly with a sharp apple flavour. The fruit is also used in tarts, combined with other hedgerow fruit, or pressed for a tart cider-style juice. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.

: confirm (1) the small, round, greenish-yellow or red-flushed fruit with a five-lobed core on cutting, (2) the spiny branches with small oval toothed leaves, and (3) the hedgerow, scrubland, or old woodland edge habitat. All three must match.
Fruit: 2 to 4 cm across, greenish-yellow, often with a red flush. Hard, acid, and very tart when raw. The core is five-lobed when cut through, the same as a cultivated apple.
Branches: spiny, with short rigid spurs that end in a thorn-like tip. An important distinguishing feature from ornamental crabs, which are usually spineless.
Leaves: small, oval, 3 to 5 cm, with a finely toothed edge and a hairless surface when mature.
Crab apple has no directly toxic UK
when fruiting; the small apple with a five-lobed core is distinctive. Ornamental crabs in parks and gardens are edible and cook the same way; their fruit is often larger.

Pick from August through October. Ripe fruit drops easily when you press upward gently; unripe fruit resists. Collect windfalls from the ground if they are fresh and undamaged; check each one for blemishes and discard any that are fermented or mouldy. Crab apple trees can be tall and branchy; collect what falls and what is reachable without climbing.

Rinse, quarter, and remove any damaged sections. For jelly, simmer in water until completely soft, then strain through a double layer of muslin without pressing (pressing clouds the jelly). Add sugar to the liquid and simmer to setting point. For juice, quarter and simmer, then strain and press through a colander lined with muslin.

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of fruit from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Crab apple trees in ancient woodland may be part of a protected hedgerow or SSSI boundary; check before picking.

rows.symptom: Jelly is cloudy rather than clear
rows.cause: Pulp was squeezed through the cloth rather than left to drip freely
rows.fix: Do not press or squeeze the muslin bag; let the juice drip overnight. Any pressing clouds the jelly permanently.

rows.symptom: Fruit is very hard even in October
rows.cause: Season running late, or a late-fruiting strain
rows.fix: Test by pressing the base of the fruit; it should give slightly when ripe. Collect windfalls as a guide to ripeness. Cook harder fruits for longer before straining.
